They are not a sphere. A "ball" of sorts is inserted during the removal surgery to fill space in the socket, and the muscles that move the eye are sewn to it. The prosthetic sits between the eyelid and the flesh that grows over that "ball", being held in only by suction and a tight fit. Therefore, the prosthesis has to be custom made to each wearer's specific socket space.

If you don't mind seeing an eyesocket without an eye, watch this short video which shows both the prosthesis and what the eye socket looks like. Plus, the chick is kinda hot. Video

Edit: hers was not "fitted" like mine was. My prosthetic eye fits perfectly to the socket ball behind it, so when I look in a specific direction, the prosthesis moves in tandem with the good eye.

Wow, that was really cool! Thanks for taking the time to explain, I've always wondered how that works. So there's a dummy 'eyeball' implanted into the socket and is moved by the existing muscles, and the cosmetic prosthetic sits on top of that and moves with it so it looks like the eye is tracking?

That is exactly what it does. The really cool part for me was, since my left eye had had so many problems (cataracts, spotty vision where I could see peripherally but not straight ahead), the eye would always be off center a bit. I had AWESOME peripheral vision to the left, though! When I got tired (or drunk!) it would tend to float to the outside (lazy eye kind of thing.) In addition, because the eye never really formed properly, it was a lighter shade of brown than my good eye, so I had one dark brown colored eye, and one light brown eye. Not enough to notice a HUGE difference like people with 1 green, 1 blue , but it was there.

Now, since the prosthesis maker hand painted the iris to match the good eye, even adding features like similar size and color veins, people I have known for years can't tell which is the good eye and which is the bad.

In terms of appearance, I actually improved!

In terms of effect, wow, you don't realize how much vision you have lost when you lose one eye. Crowds, supermarkets, airports, etc. and a minefield for me of bumping into people that I just didn't see. Driving sucks now. I hate it. I have to do a 100-120 degree turn of the head just to check my blindside. I set up my mirrors WAY out to the left, so that when a car is passing me on the left (which is the only place a car should ever be passing you), as it leaves the rearview mirror, it will be appearing in the side mirror. By the time it begins leaving the side mirror, I should be able to see it without a large head swivel, just a glance over out the driver side window. What i really need is a Right hand drive car.
That is awesome, I've always wondered how prosthetic eyes work. Thanks!

No worries, glad to impart my experiences!

What was even cooler was watching them hand paint the eye in front of me, matching colors.

They used a series of thin paintbrush strokes on a metallic disc, starting with silver, then moving to gold, with the effect of the combined silver and gold forming the way a brown eye looks (more gold than silver) while a blue eye has almost all silver, and a green eye is roughly half and half.

They added a touch of yellow and blue to each gold and silver to accentuate the colors, since it is really only a flat disc, while a real eye has layers and is curved. They then finished with a thin coat of brown to overlay and match my other eye perfectly.

For the blood vessels, they actually took a thin red thread, and scrape with an exacto knife to "shred" it into the shape of connected blood vessels. The artist even used some of the "chaff" form the scraping to give the "white" part less of a bright white color, and a more realistic color of eyeball.

I say artist, because the ocularist (ocu-artist!) who did this was amazingly good at their job.
